title: NASA asks industry how to save Hubble: boost it, service it, or bring it down safely
excerpt: NASA is asking private companies how they could save the Hubble Space Telescope — boost it to a higher orbit, service it, or bring it down in a controlled reent
content:
NASA is asking private companies how they could save the Hubble Space Telescope — boost it to a higher orbit, service it, or bring it down in a controlled reentry — before atmospheric drag pulls it out of the sky in the early 2030s.

The agency issued a Request for Information on October 29, 2026, through NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, posted as notice 80GSFC27RFIHSTS on SAM.gov. Responses are due by 3 p.m. Eastern on Monday, November 30.

The notice lays out three options. A company could develop a servicing vehicle that captures Hubble in low Earth orbit and boosts it to at least 600 kilometers (373 miles). It could fly a servicing mission to enhance the observatory's performance and increase its resilience and expected lifetime. Or it could fly a mission for a controlled reentry or orbital disposal at the end of Hubble's mission.

An RFI is not a contract, a funded mission, or a commitment to buy anything. NASA says it is gathering information on what companies can do now or in the near term, and at what cost, before deciding anything. A formal request for proposals could follow, but no date has been set.

The urgency is orbital mechanics. Hubble has no propulsion system of its own, and atmospheric drag is slowly lowering its orbit. NASA says analysis predicts Hubble is likely to reenter the atmosphere in the 2033 to 2034 timeframe, so any boost or disposal mission would need to take place by 2032. A July 2026 lifetime analysis cited in reporting on the notice put the modeled probability of reentry at 10% by September 2032 and 50% by December 2033.

Hubble was deployed in April 1990 and last had its orbit raised in 2002, when the Space Shuttle Columbia visited it for servicing. A 2022 proposal from Jared Isaacman's Polaris Program and SpaceX to reboost Hubble with a Crew Dragon capsule was studied by NASA and declined in 2024, over concerns including the risk to Hubble's ultraviolet-sensitive mirrors. Isaacman is now NASA's administrator, and in the agency's announcement he said, "Hubble still has important science ahead of it, and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible."

For readers in Webb County, Hubble's story is a reminder that even the most famous instruments need maintenance — and that the decision about whether to spend money saving a 36-year-old telescope, or to let it burn up, is now an open question NASA has put to industry, with answers due November 30.

Sources:

  • NASA, "NASA Explores Potential Commercial Servicing for Hubble Telescope," October 30, 2026
  • Gizmodo, "NASA's Begging the Commercial Space Industry to Save the Doomed Hubble Telescope," October 31, 2026
  • The Vanguard USA, "NASA asks companies to boost Hubble to 600 km by 2032," October 2026 (reporting notice 80GSFC27RFIHSTS)
